What
                                                                                      is a                    Seismic
                           Survey                ?




First, a survey crew will move down roads or across open
fields to gather surface measurements and details. These
measurements determine where to place the series of cables
equipped with geophones. Once the geophones are placed,
trucks move in tandem down the road or through an area
lowering a vibration pad onto the surface every few feet. The
waves generated travel deep underground and are reflected
back as echoes from the different rock layers. The reflections
are picked up by a recording truck, which captures the data
for computer processing and analysis.


                                                                                                                     Image Courtesy of Schlumberger
By measuring the time it takes a vibration to reach a rock
layer and be reflected back to the surface, the depths of
the rock layers can be determined, and an image of the
subsurface can be formed. Once the seismic survey data has
been collected, any surface sign that the survey has taken
place is repaired and within a few short weeks everything is
back to the way it was. The subsurface image is created from
the data collected which an interpreter then uses to define
the shape of the rock layers, how continuous they are, and
what type of rock is present. The interpreter also must use
data from nearby deep wells to validate the interpretation.
